analogy.p: Imagine you wiggle the end of a long rope up and down (the transmitter). A wave runs along the rope at a steady speed, and a cork tied further along (the receiver) bobs up and down at exactly the same rate you wiggled. The cork's motion has the same frequency as your hand, which matches an induced AC having the same frequency as the AC in the transmitter. The analogy breaks down because radio waves need no rope or medium and travel through a vacuum, and nothing like the rope moves along; also the wave spreads out in all directions instead of one line.
analogy.t: A rope and a floating cork

bullets: **Production:** an **alternating current** (oscillating charges) in a **transmitter circuit and aerial** makes radio waves.
**Absorption:** radio waves hitting a **receiver aerial** make **electrons oscillate**, creating an **alternating current of the same frequency**.
The frequency of the wave = the frequency of the AC that produced it = the frequency of the AC it induces.
Energy is transferred from the transmitter's supply to the receiver by the wave.
This content is **Higher tier only**; Foundation students only learn the uses of radio waves.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (Higher tier)
core.p: At Higher tier you must explain how **radio waves are produced and detected using electrical circuits**. Radio waves can be **produced by oscillations in electrical circuits**. When radio waves are **absorbed**, they may **create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio waves themselves**, so radio waves can themselves **induce oscillations in an electrical circuit**. This is the principle behind every radio, TV and mobile phone link: a transmitter turns an alternating current into waves, and a receiver turns the waves back into an alternating current. The key phrase to learn is **'same frequency'**.

bullets: **Frequency** (Hz) = number of cycles per second; **period** (s) = time for one cycle; **f = 1 / T**, **T = 1 / f**.
A 50 Hz mains supply has period T = 1 / 50 = **0.02 s**.
**Prefixes:** 1 kHz = 10^3 Hz, 1 MHz = 10^6 Hz, 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz.
An oscilloscope trace of AC is a **wave**; read the period from the time axis (e.g. horizontal distance of one wave x time per division).
In an AC circuit, the **electrons oscillate to and fro** around a fixed position rather than travelling round the circuit.
AC can be **tuned** to a precise frequency using an **oscillator circuit**.
core.p: An **alternating current (AC)** is a current that **repeatedly reverses direction** (the charge flows one way, then the other). **Direct current (DC)** flows in one direction only. The **frequency** of an AC is the number of complete cycles per second, in **hertz (Hz)**, and the **period** T is the time for one cycle, with **f = 1 / T**. UK mains is AC at **50 Hz** and **230 V**. Signals in radio circuits are AC at far higher frequencies, from thousands to hundreds of millions of hertz.

bullets: Step 1: oscillator circuit makes **AC of frequency f**.
Step 2: AC passes to the **aerial**; electrons **oscillate** along it at frequency f.
Step 3: oscillating (accelerating) charges produce **changing electric and magnetic fields**, which travel away as an **EM (radio) wave**.
Step 4: the wave has **frequency f**, speed 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in air or vacuum, and wavelength = speed / f.
The wave transfers energy **away from the aerial** to anything that later absorbs it.
**Why oscillation matters:** a steady direct current in a wire does **not** radiate waves; changing (accelerating) charge is needed.
core.p: A **transmitter** has an **oscillator circuit** that creates an alternating current at the chosen frequency. This current is fed to the **transmitting aerial** (a metal rod or wire). The **electrons in the aerial are repeatedly accelerated** backwards and forwards. Accelerating charges produce **changing electric and magnetic fields** that spread outwards as an **electromagnetic wave**. The wave has the **same frequency** as the oscillations of the electrons because each oscillation of the charges produces one wave. Energy is carried away from the aerial at **3.0 x 10^8 m/s**.

bullets: The induced AC has the **same frequency** as the radio wave that produced it.
The size of the induced current is **very small** and decreases with distance from the transmitter, so receivers use **amplifiers**.
The receiver aerial must be a **conductor** (e.g. metal) so electrons can move.
Energy is **absorbed** from the wave and ends up as electrical energy in the receiver circuit.
Aerials work best when **oriented correctly** (e.g. vertical aerial for a vertically polarised signal).
**Link to electromagnetism:** a changing field making charges move is the same idea as electromagnetic induction.
core.h: How radio waves are absorbed and detected
core.p: When a radio wave reaches a **receiving aerial** (a conductor), the **electric field of the wave pushes the electrons** in the metal to and fro. Because the field of the wave oscillates at frequency f, the electrons are made to oscillate at the **same frequency f**, which is an **alternating current in the receiver circuit**. This current is tiny, so it is **amplified**, and the useful signal is processed to produce **sound or a picture**. This is also called **induction**: the wave induces oscillations in a circuit.

bullets: **Transmitter chain:** microphone, oscillator (carrier), amplifier, aerial.
**Receiver chain:** aerial, tuner, amplifier, loudspeaker.
A **microphone** converts sound to an AC signal; a **loudspeaker** converts AC to sound.
Only the **frequency** is shared between the wave and the AC; the wave is transverse and the current is moving electrons.
A single transmitter can reach **many receivers**; every aerial in range gets an induced AC.
Energy transfers: electrical store of supply, to waves, to electrical energy in the receiver, to sound energy.
core.h: Transmitter and receiver as a matched pair
core.p: Think of the whole link as a chain with the same frequency running through it. At the transmitter: sound is turned into an electrical signal, combined with a high-frequency **carrier** AC, amplified and fed to the aerial. At the receiver: the aerial gives a weak AC, the **tuner** selects the wanted frequency, the signal is amplified, the sound signal is recovered, and the **loudspeaker** turns the electrical signal back into sound. Each stage changes the form of energy, but the **frequency** of the carrier is the same at both aerials.

bullets: The aerial gives a **mixture** of alternating currents of many frequencies.
The **tuner** selects the frequency you want and rejects the rest.
If a tuner is set to 94.0 MHz, the circuit responds to AC at 94.0 MHz.
Stations broadcasting on the **same frequency** in the same area cause interference.
This is why the induced current must have **exactly the same frequency** as the transmitted wave for the receiver to work.
Digital radios and mobile phones do the same job with more complex electronics.
core.p: An aerial picks up **all** the radio waves arriving at it, from many stations at once, so the receiver must **select one frequency**. A **tuning circuit** responds strongly only to AC of one particular frequency (it is in **resonance** with it) and responds weakly to others. Turning the tuning dial changes the frequency the circuit prefers. Stations are given **different frequencies** so that signals do not interfere.

bullets: **Carrier wave:** constant high frequency radio wave from the oscillator.
**AM:** amplitude of carrier changes with the sound signal; **FM:** frequency changes.
**Demodulation** at the receiver recovers the audio signal from the carrier.
Digital signals use patterns of pulses (on/off) to carry data.
Not required for the specification; focus on production and absorption with the same frequency.
FM is less affected by electrical noise than AM.
core.h: Putting information onto a radio wave (modulation, extension)
core.p: A speech or music signal is at **audio frequency** (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz), which is too low to be radiated well. So a **high-frequency carrier wave** is used, and the information is added by **modulation**. In **AM** (amplitude modulation) the **amplitude** of the carrier varies with the sound; in **FM** (frequency modulation) the **frequency** of the carrier varies slightly. The receiver **demodulates** the signal to recover the sound. This detail goes beyond the specification but explains why radio works.

bullets: **Long wavelength:** diffracts more, so better reception behind obstacles.
**Ionosphere reflection** helps long-distance reception for lower frequencies (extension).
**Line of sight** for VHF/UHF (FM radio, TV); relay stations and satellites extend the range.
**Wave equation** works for all: v = f x wavelength.
Radio waves can pass through **walls** with some absorption; thick metal reflects them.
Signal strength falls with distance because energy **spreads out** over a larger area.
core.h: Radio wave properties and how far they travel
core.p: Radio waves are **transverse EM waves** that travel at **3.0 x 10^8 m/s** in a vacuum (and nearly so in air). Wavelengths range from about **0.1 m to over 10 km**. Long wavelengths **diffract** round hills and buildings and some are **reflected by the ionosphere**, so they travel long distances; shorter radio waves (such as FM and TV) travel in straight lines and need **line of sight** or relay masts. Radio waves are **non-ionising**.

bullets: Example: a 94.0 MHz FM station: f = 9.40 x 10^7 Hz; wavelength = 3.0 x 10^8 / 9.40 x 10^7 = **3.2 m**.
Example: Radio 4 long wave 198 kHz = 1.98 x 10^5 Hz; wavelength = 3.0 x 10^8 / 1.98 x 10^5 = **1500 m** (1515 m unrounded).
Example: period 2.0 microseconds = 2.0 x 10^-6 s; f = 1 / 2.0 x 10^-6 = **5.0 x 10^5 Hz**.
Check: the **higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength** (speed is constant).
Include **units** and standard form; quote 2 significant figures if data is to 2 s.f.
Mains 50 Hz would have a wavelength of 3.0 x 10^8 / 50 = 6.0 x 10^6 m (6000 km), which is why mains wiring is a very poor radio transmitter.
core.h: Calculations with frequency, period and wavelength
core.p: Two equations do almost all the work: **wave speed v = f x wavelength** (m/s = Hz x m) with v = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s for radio waves, and **f = 1 / T**. Always convert frequency to **hertz** first. Rearranged: **wavelength = v / f** and **f = v / wavelength**.

bullets: Short wavelength means a **short aerial** works; long wavelength means a **tall mast**.
A **dish** can focus short wavelength waves (microwaves) into a beam.
A stronger transmitter (more power) gives a **larger amplitude** wave and a larger induced current.
The induced current falls the further the receiver is from the transmitter.
Metal buildings can **shield** receivers and weaken the signal.
Not examined in detail; use only as a supporting explanation.
core.p: A transmitting aerial radiates well when its **length is comparable to the wavelength** (often half or a quarter of it). That is why a mobile phone, which uses short wavelength signals, can have a tiny aerial but a long-wave radio needs a huge mast. A receiving aerial likewise picks up most signal when its length is matched to the wavelength. This idea is not on the specification but helps explain why different systems use different frequencies.

bullets: Radio waves cannot **ionise** atoms, so no gene mutation like X-rays.
Safety limits keep exposure low for those working near transmitters.
Typical uses: **television and radio** broadcasting.
Mobile phones and Wi-Fi use higher-frequency waves (microwave region) with the same principle.
The principle **AC in a circuit to wave to AC** is used in all wireless communication.
Don't confuse radio waves with **radioactivity**: radio waves are non-ionising EM waves.
core.p: Radio waves are at the **low-energy, low-frequency end** of the spectrum, are **non-ionising**, and are not known to cause mutation or cancer at normal broadcast levels. Very high power transmitters could heat tissue, so people are kept away from the aerials. Everyday devices that use radio-frequency AC include radios, TVs, walkie-talkies, remote controls and many wireless systems.

bullets: **Electromagnetism:** a changing current produces a changing magnetic field; the reverse can induce a potential difference.
**Energy:** energy is transferred electrically to the aerial, by the wave, then electrically to the receiver circuit.
**Spectrum:** all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum; radio has the lowest frequency.
**Sound:** a microphone and loudspeaker convert between sound and AC.
**Uses of EM waves:** TV and radio are the main uses of radio waves.
**Data skills:** oscilloscope traces, reading period, calculating f and wavelength.
core.p: This point ties together waves, electricity and magnetism. It uses the **wave equation**, **alternating current** from the electricity topic, and the idea of **induction** from the magnetism topic: a changing electric current produces changing fields, and changing fields make charges move. It also links to the spectrum point, where you learn that **changes in atoms and nuclei** emit other parts of the EM spectrum, whereas radio waves come from oscillating electric circuits.

bullets: Marking points: AC/oscillations in transmitter circuit; electrons in aerial oscillate; radio wave produced of same frequency; wave absorbed by receiver aerial; electrons oscillate; AC of same frequency induced.
Use the phrase **'induces an alternating current of the same frequency as the radio wave'**.
Do not say the radio wave 'is' the current; the wave **causes** the current.
Mention **energy transfer** where asked (from the wave to the circuit).
For calculations, show the equation, substitution, and unit.
Draw and label diagrams with aerial, circuit and direction of the wave.
core.h: How to write a Higher-tier answer
core.p: Examiners expect a **sequence** with the key words **'alternating current'**, **'oscillate'**, **'same frequency'**, **'absorbed'** and **'induces'**. Write the transmitter story first and then the receiver, and state the frequency link at both stages. A 4-mark answer needs about four distinct points; a 6-mark answer should be ordered and complete.

exam: **Command words:** 'describe how radio waves are produced' needs a sequence: AC in circuit, electrons oscillate in the aerial, radio wave emitted.
**1 mark:** a single fact, e.g. 'the induced current has the same frequency'.
**2 marks:** a fact with a reason, e.g. 'an alternating current in the aerial makes electrons oscillate, which produces the wave'.
**4 marks:** cover both production and absorption, mentioning 'alternating current', 'oscillate' and 'same frequency'.
**6 marks:** a logical chain from transmitter to receiver including tuning, amplification and sound output, with a final statement of frequency matching.
**Calculations:** write the equation, convert units (kHz or MHz to Hz), substitute, give answer with unit.
**Trace questions:** use the horizontal scale to get the period, then use f = 1 / T.
**Use exact phrases:** 'induces', 'alternating current of the same frequency', 'oscillations in an electrical circuit'.
**Avoid** saying the wave 'travels along the wire' or that electrons travel through the air.
**Higher-tier check:** if a question mentions 'induce' or 'electrical circuit', this is the content being tested.

mistakes.r: Radio waves are produced by oscillations: an alternating current in the transmitter circuit and aerial.
mistakes.w: Radio waves are produced by a steady current in the aerial.

mistakes.r: The wave has the same frequency as the alternating current that produced it.
mistakes.w: The radio wave has a different frequency from the current that made it.

mistakes.r: The receiver aerial absorbs the wave and an alternating current of the same frequency is induced in it.
mistakes.w: The receiver aerial makes the radio wave.

mistakes.r: Electrons only oscillate in the aerials; the energy is carried between them by the radio wave.
mistakes.w: Electrons travel from the transmitter to the receiver.

mistakes.r: Radio waves are transverse EM waves and can travel through a vacuum; sound waves are longitudinal and need a medium.
Convert to hertz first (1 MHz = 10^6 Hz) so the units match m/s.
mistakes.w: Frequency in MHz can be put straight into v = f x wavelength.

mistakes.r: Radio waves are non-ionising; radioactivity is a nuclear process.
mistakes.w: Radio waves are radioactive or ionising.

mistakes.r: The tuner selects one frequency; the wave speed is fixed at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
mistakes.w: The tuner changes the speed of the wave.

summary: At Higher tier you must explain that radio waves are produced by oscillations in electrical circuits and that, when radio waves are absorbed, they create an alternating current of the same frequency as the wave. It matters because it explains how every radio, TV and wireless link transmits and receives information.

terms.d: A current which repeatedly reverses direction.
A current which flows in one direction only.
The number of waves passing a point per second, or cycles of an AC per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete cycle; T = 1 / f.
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz is one wave or cycle per second.
A repeated to-and-fro movement, such as electrons moving back and forth in an aerial.
EM waves with the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.
A conductor in which oscillating electrons produce radio waves, or in which radio waves induce an alternating current.
The device and circuit that produces radio waves.
The device that absorbs radio waves and produces an electrical signal from them.
To cause a current or potential difference in a conductor, here by absorbed radio waves.
A circuit that selects one frequency and rejects others.
A high-frequency wave onto which information is added.
Changing the amplitude or frequency of a carrier wave to carry information (extension).
The speed at which a wave transfers energy; for EM waves in a vacuum, 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
The distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
Not having enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, as with radio waves.

worked.q: An oscilloscope trace of the alternating current in a transmitter shows one complete wave takes 2.0 microseconds. Calculate the frequency and the wavelength of the radio waves produced. (4 marks)

worked.ans: An alternating current in the transmitter circuit makes electrons oscillate in the aerial, producing radio waves of the same frequency. When these waves are absorbed by the receiver aerial they induce an alternating current of the same frequency in the receiver circuit.
worked.q: Explain how a radio transmitter produces radio waves and how a receiver detects them. (4 marks)
steps: An alternating current (oscillations) in the transmitter circuit makes electrons oscillate in the aerial.
This produces radio waves with the same frequency as the alternating current.
The waves are absorbed by the receiver aerial.
This makes electrons oscillate, inducing an alternating current of the same frequency in the receiver circuit.
